### Problem: Badge {#sec-gr-p5-badge}

There are $n$ students, $1$-indexed. Student $p_i$ is the one $i$ points at, and every student points at exactly one student, who may be themselves. For each start $s$, print the first student who appears twice on the walk that begins at $s$.

**Graph model.** Functional, $n \le 1000$. The answer for $s$ is the entrance of the cycle reached from $s$. A student on the cycle is their own answer.

**Invariants.** A fresh "seen" array per start is correct, and at $n \le 1000$ it is fast enough: $O(n^2)$. The linear form peels every vertex of in-degree $0$, repeatedly. What remains is the cycles. Each cycle vertex answers itself. Every other vertex copies the answer of the first cycle vertex it can reach.

**Approaches.**

1. **Resimulate** — one boolean array per start. The form to submit at this limit, and the definition of the sample.
2. **Peel, then copy** — $O(n)$. The same answers, and the form to reuse when $n \le 10^5$.

::: {#fig-gr-p5-badge}

```{python}

            note="cycle vertices answer themselves")
V.show(draw)
```

$p = (2, 3, 2)$. The walk $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 2$ repeats $2$. The walk $3 \to 2 \to 3$ repeats $3$.

:::

::: {.panel-tabset .solution-forms}

#### Resimulate

::: {.form-next}
From each start, walk until the current student is already on this walk. That student is the answer.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("badge", "sim")
    assert str(final) == "[2, 2, 3]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def badge(p):
    n = len(p) - 1
    ans = [0] * (n + 1)
    for s in range(1, n + 1):
        seen = [False] * (n + 1)
        v = s
        while not seen[v]:
            seen[v] = True
            v = p[v]
        ans[s] = v
    return ans[1:]


assert badge([0, 2, 3, 2]) == [2, 2, 3]
assert badge([0, 1, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3]
assert badge([0, 2, 3, 4, 2, 4, 7, 8, 6, 5]) == [2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 7, 8, 4]
assert badge([0, 2, 3, 4, 4]) == [4, 4, 4, 4]
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<int> badge(vector<int>& p) {
    int n = (int)p.size() - 1;
    vector<int> ans(n + 1);
    for (int s = 1; s <= n; s++) {
        vector<char> seen(n + 1);
        int v = s;
        while (!seen[v]) {
            seen[v] = 1;
            v = p[v];
        }
        ans[s] = v;
    }
    return vector<int>(ans.begin() + 1, ans.end());
}
```

:::

#### Peel, then copy

::: {.form-next}
Vertices that survive the in-degree peel are on cycles and answer themselves. A tail vertex takes the answer of the cycle vertex it reaches.
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| renderings: [light, dark]
def draw(ax, p):
    title, inp, steps, final = Traces.get("badge", "peel")
    assert str(final) == "[2, 2, 3]"
    V.story(ax, p, title, inp, steps, final)
V.show(draw)
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="lang"}

##### Python

```{python}
def badge_linear(p):
    n = len(p) - 1
    indeg = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        indeg[p[i]] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(1, n + 1) if indeg[i] == 0)
    on_cycle = [True] * (n + 1)
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        on_cycle[u] = False
        indeg[p[u]] -= 1
        if indeg[p[u]] == 0:
            q.append(p[u])
    ans = [0] * (n + 1)
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        if on_cycle[i]:
            ans[i] = i
    for i in range(1, n + 1):
        if ans[i]:
            continue
        path = []
        v = i
        while not ans[v]:
            path.append(v)
            v = p[v]
        for u in path:
            ans[u] = ans[v]
    return ans[1:]


assert badge_linear([0, 2, 3, 2]) == [2, 2, 3]
assert badge_linear([0, 1, 2, 3]) == [1, 2, 3]
assert badge_linear([0, 2, 3, 4, 2, 4, 7, 8, 6, 5]) == [2, 2, 3, 4, 4, 6, 7, 8, 4]
assert badge_linear([0, 2, 3, 4, 4]) == [4, 4, 4, 4]
for n in range(1, 12):
    for _ in range(20):
        p = [0] + [random.randint(1, n) for _ in range(n)]
        assert badge(p) == badge_linear(p)
```

##### C++

```cpp
vector<int> badgeLinear(vector<int>& p) {
    int n = (int)p.size() - 1;
    vector<int> indeg(n + 1), ans(n + 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) indeg[p[i]]++;
    queue<int> q;
    vector<char> on(n + 1, 1);
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        if (indeg[i] == 0) q.push(i);
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front();
        q.pop();
        on[u] = 0;
        if (--indeg[p[u]] == 0) q.push(p[u]);
    }
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++)
        if (on[i]) ans[i] = i;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) {
        if (ans[i]) continue;
        vector<int> path;
        int v = i;
        while (!ans[v]) {
            path.push_back(v);
            v = p[v];
        }
        for (int u : path) ans[u] = ans[v];
    }
    return vector<int>(ans.begin() + 1, ans.end());
}
```

:::

:::

**Worked trace.** $p = (2, 3, 2)$. Student $3$ lies on the cycle $2 \to 3 \to 2$, so the answer at $3$ is $3$. Writing $2$ into every vertex of that cycle is the mistake: the walk that starts at $3$ repeats $3$, not $2$.

**Edge cases.** $n$ self-loops: each student answers themselves. A chain $1 \to 2 \to 3 \to 4 \to 4$: everyone answers $4$. The length-$9$ sample has two cycles, $\{2, 3, 4\}$ and $\{6, 7, 8\}$, and the tails $1$, $5$, and $9 \to 5$ answer the cycle entrance they hit.

**Pitfalls.** $p$ is $1$-indexed; a vector of length $n$ shifts every successor. Setting the answer of a whole path to the first repeated student is right for the tail and wrong for the cycle vertices further along, who each repeat themselves. At $n \le 1000$ the quadratic resimulation is inside the limit; the linear form is what you want when the same model appears with $n \le 10^5$.

::: {.callout-warning title="Common mistakes"}
- **One seen array for every start.** The second walk then stops on a student who was marked during the first. Each start is its own experiment.
- **Stopping one student early.** The answer is the student who is already on this walk, not the student who pointed at them.
- **Painting the whole path with the entrance.** On $2 \to 3 \to 2$ the cycle vertex $3$ repeats itself. Copying $2$ onto every vertex of the path answers $2, 2, 2$. The sample wants $2, 2, 3$.
:::

**Variants.** The length of the longest cycle, instead of the entrance of each walk, is @sec-gr-p5-cycle. One start and $K$ up to $10^{18}$ steps is [AC abc167_d · Teleporter](https://atcoder.jp/contests/abc167/tasks/abc167_d): the same tail and cycle, then a modular step along the cycle. The number of distinct students a start holes is the tail length plus the cycle length. Paying for the cheapest vertex on every cycle, so that every walk is eventually caught, is [CF 1027D · Mouse Hunt](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1027/D){rating="1700"}.

Source: [CF 1020B · Badge](https://codeforces.com/problemset/problem/1020/B){.solved rating="1000"}
